Goad
GOHD
n.
Old English gād, “spear, point”; a sharp pointed stick used to drive oxen at the plow. Hebrew málmād (ox-goad; Judges 3:31, Shamgar’s weapon) and dōrbān / dárbōn; Greek kentron (goad; Acts 26:14, kick against the pricks).

Biblical Definition

The goad is a sharp pointed stick used in ancient agriculture to drive oxen at the plow—a small pointed implement (sometimes brass-tipped) the plowman jabbed against the ox’s flank to keep the animal moving in the proper direction. The goad has several distinct biblical uses. First, the literal-agricultural and improvised-military use. Judges 3:31 records Shamgar son of Anath, who slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad: and he also delivered Israel. The ox-goad as an improvised weapon in the hand of a deliverer became one of the OT’s vivid demonstrations of God’s using the humblest of instruments for the rescue of His people. 1 Samuel 13:21 mentions a file for the mattocks, and for the coulters, and for the forks, and for the axes, and to sharpen the goads—the goads were maintained tools of the agricultural economy, requiring sharpening. Second, the wise-words use. Ecclesiastes 12:11: the words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. The Preacher likens wise words to two things: goads that prick the conscience and drive the soul toward right action, and nails that fasten truth securely in the mind. The wise-words goad is therefore the pricking, conscience-stirring, action-prompting effect of the truth spoken under God’s appointment. Third, the supreme New Testament use. Acts 26:14, where Christ on the Damascus road says to Saul: Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. The Greek behind pricks is kentron—the goads. The image is of the ox kicking against the plowman’s goad: the more the ox kicks, the more it impales itself; the resistance to the goad only intensifies the wound. Christ’s diagnosis of Saul’s pre-conversion persecution of the church is precise: Saul has been resisting the conviction of God’s prods (the testimony of Stephen, the witness of the Christians he persecuted, his own conscience under the conviction of the truth), and every kick against the goads has only deepened his self-wound. The phrase kick against the pricks has entered English from this single biblical use as the proverbial description of resistance against what is in the end the resister’s own good. The goad-doctrine therefore carries substantial theological substance: the LORD’s use of humble instruments for great deliverances (Shamgar); the wise word as the conscience-pricking, action-driving truth (Ecclesiastes 12:11); and the futility of kicking against the divine goads that are in the end for the resister’s own salvation (Christ to Saul). The pastoral application is direct: when the LORD’s goads prick the conscience (through Scripture, through providence, through faithful preaching, through the witness of the Spirit), the wise response is not to kick against them but to turn in their direction, lest the kicking only deepen the wound.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines GOAD as a pointed instrument used to stimulate beasts to move faster; in scripture, Shamgar’s 600-Philistine-slaying ox-goad (Judg 3:31), the Preacher’s wise-words-as-goads (Eccl 12:11), and Christ’s Damascus-road diagnosis of Saul: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks (Acts 26:14).

GOAD, n. — A pointed instrument used to stimulate beasts to move faster, particularly oxen at the plow. In scripture, both the literal agricultural tool and the figurative pricking-instrument of the LORD’s conviction.

PRICK, n. — A slender pointed thing; in the KJV, often the same as goad; the “pricks” against which Christ told Saul it was hard to kick (Acts 26:14).

Key Scripture

Acts 26:14 — "And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks."

Ecclesiastes 12:11 — "The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd."

Judges 3:31 — "And after him was Shamgar the son of Anath, which slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad: and he also delivered Israel."

1 Samuel 13:21 — "Yet they had a file for the mattocks, and for the coulters, and for the forks, and for the axes, and to sharpen the goads."

Modern Corruption

The goad-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the loss of the divine-conviction-as-goad register in much contemporary preaching that has muted the substantive teaching of Christ’s Damascus-road diagnosis (the futility of kicking against the LORD’s prods)—and by the inverse over-extension that has used the kick-against-the-pricks language to label every form of disagreement as resistance against God, without the careful discernment Christ’s actual diagnosis of Saul required.

expand to see more

The loss of the divine-conviction-as-goad register has muted one of the more substantive pastoral teachings of the New Testament. Christ’s diagnosis of Saul on the Damascus road is precise: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. Saul had been resisting the LORD’s prods—the testimony of Stephen (Acts 7), the witness of the Christians he persecuted, his own conscience under the conviction of the truth. Each act of resistance had only deepened the self-wound; the more Saul kicked, the more impaled he became. The contemporary application is direct: when the LORD’s goads prick the conscience through Scripture, faithful preaching, the witness of the Spirit, or providential dealing, the wise response is to turn in the direction of the prick rather than to kick against it. Resistance only deepens the wound; submission allows the goad to do its salvation-producing work. The recovery is the recovery of attention to the LORD’s goads in the believer’s own life and to the goad-warning Christ Himself gave to the persecuting Saul.

The opposite corruption is the over-extension of the kick-against-the-pricks language to label every form of disagreement as resistance against God. The pattern often appears in spiritual-abuse contexts: when a believer questions a leader, raises concerns about doctrine or practice, or refuses to comply with an instruction, the leader invokes Acts 26:14 to characterize the dissent as kicking-against-divine-pricks. The label is rhetorically effective and theologically illegitimate. Christ’s diagnosis of Saul required careful discernment that the resistance was indeed against the LORD’s own prods (the testimony of Stephen, the witness of the church, the truth of the gospel)—not against any human authority claiming divine sanction. Recover the careful discernment: the kick-against-the-pricks warning applies to resistance against the actual LORD’s actual goads, identifiable as such by their alignment with Scripture and the work of the Spirit, not to every form of dissent against human authority that invokes the divine. The biblical goad-doctrine is direct and pastorally rich—the LORD prods toward salvation and obedience, and the wise saint yields rather than kicks—but the application requires the careful discernment Christ Himself modeled in the precise diagnosis He gave to Saul of his actual resistance against the actual divine truth he had been opposing.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew málmād (ox-goad; Judg 3:31), dōrbān / dárbōn (goad; Eccl 12:11; 1 Sam 13:21); Greek kentron (goad, point; Acts 26:14’s pricks); the agricultural ox-prod, used by Shamgar as improvised weapon, by the Preacher as image of wise words’ conscience-pricking, and by Christ as diagnosis of Saul’s pre-conversion futile resistance against the LORD’s salvation-producing prods.

Hebrew málmād (H4451) — ox-goad (Judg 3:31, Shamgar’s weapon).

Hebrew dōrbān / dárbōn (H1861) — goad (Eccl 12:11; 1 Sam 13:21).

Greek kentron (G2759) — goad, sting, point (Acts 26:14; 1 Cor 15:55-56; Rev 9:10).

Greek laktizō (G2979) — to kick (Acts 26:14, to kick against the pricks).
